Geospatial Data Wrangling with R

Author

Davin Cuaso

Published

6 September 2026

Modified

14 September 2026

Overview

I worked through Chapter 1: Geospatial Data Science with R using the current public downloads. The steps cover importing, checking, projecting, converting and geoprocessing spatial data in R. I use them to answer two practical questions:

  1. How much land lies within five metres of Singapore’s cycling-path network?
  2. How are pre-schools distributed across Master Plan 2014 subzones?

Data and packages

The files now supplied through data.gov.sg are GeoJSON rather than the shapefile and KML formats used in the original course notes. I used GeoJSON because it is the official downloadable format and keeps each layer’s geometry in one file.

The requested Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) collection currently has no downloadable child dataset, so I used Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (No Sea). For the pre-school density calculation, this is a reasonable substitute because offshore polygons add area but no pre-school points.

Dataset Source Format Purpose
Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) URA via data.gov.sg GeoJSON Analysis zones
Cycling Path Network LTA via data.gov.sg GeoJSON Buffer analysis
Pre-Schools Location ECDA via data.gov.sg GeoJSON Point-in-polygon counts
Singapore Airbnb listings, 28 Dec 2024 Inside Airbnb CSV Aspatial-to-spatial conversion

The required packages are loaded with pacman::p_load(): sf manages spatial data, dplyr wrangles tables, ggplot2 plots the results, knitr formats tables, and units handles area conversions safely.

Importing geospatial data

st_read() reads all three vector datasets as simple-feature data frames. The course’s chap01/data/... path belongs to the lecturer’s project; the paths below match this repository.

Show the R code 
mpsz <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

cyclingpath <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "CyclingPathNetwork.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

preschool <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "PreSchoolsLocation.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

Inspecting the feature data frames

I first check the number of features, geometry type, attributes and coordinate reference system (CRS).

Show the R code 
spatial_summary <- data.frame(
  Object = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  Features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(cyclingpath), nrow(preschool)),
  Attributes = c(ncol(mpsz) - 1, ncol(cyclingpath) - 1, ncol(preschool) - 1),
  Geometry = c(
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(mpsz))), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(cyclingpath))), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(preschool))), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  `Native CRS` = c(st_crs(mpsz)$input, st_crs(cyclingpath)$input, st_crs(preschool)$input),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(spatial_summary, caption = "Imported geospatial datasets")
Imported geospatial datasets
Object Features Attributes Geometry Native CRS
Planning subzones 323 13 MULTIPOLYGON WGS 84
Cycling paths 8523 6 MULTILINESTRING WGS 84
Pre-schools 2290 2 POINT WGS 84

The objects contain polygon, line, and point geometries respectively. All three arrive in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), whose coordinates are measured in degrees.

Show the R code 
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz, fill = "#f5f7fa", color = "#b8c2cc", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = cyclingpath, color = "#2a9d8f", linewidth = 0.18, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = preschool, color = "#d1495b", size = 0.25, alpha = 0.55) +
  labs(
    title = "The three spatial layers align in WGS84",
    subtitle = "Subzones (grey), cycling paths (green), and pre-schools (red)"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

Working with projection

Distance and area should not be calculated in longitude and latitude. I transform all three objects to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414), a projected CRS measured in metres.

Show the R code 
mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, crs = 3414)
cyclingpath <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)
preschool <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)

crs_check <- data.frame(
  Object = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  EPSG = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(cyclingpath)$epsg, st_crs(preschool)$epsg),
  Units = c("metres", "metres", "metres")
)

kable(crs_check, caption = "CRS after transformation")
CRS after transformation
Object EPSG Units
Planning subzones 3414 metres
Cycling paths 3414 metres
Pre-schools 3414 metres

st_transform() recalculates the coordinates in a new CRS. st_set_crs() only changes the CRS label and should be used only when the coordinates were already expressed in that CRS but were labelled incorrectly.

Importing and converting aspatial data

The Airbnb CSV contains longitude and latitude fields but no geometry column, so it begins as an ordinary data frame.

Show the R code 
listings <- read.csv(
  file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "listings.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

listings_sf <- st_as_sf(
  listings,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
) |>
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

listing_summary <- data.frame(
  Records = nrow(listings_sf),
  Geometry = paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(listings_sf))), collapse = ", "),
  EPSG = st_crs(listings_sf)$epsg,
  `Longitude/latitude retained` = all(c("longitude", "latitude") %in% names(listings_sf)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(listing_summary, caption = "Airbnb data after conversion to a spatial object")
Airbnb data after conversion to a spatial object
Records Geometry EPSG Longitude/latitude retained
3447 POINT 3414 TRUE

The coordinate order is longitude, latitude (x, y). Reversing it would place the observations far outside Singapore. The converted object contains 3,447 point features in EPSG:3414.

Geoprocessing

Question 1: How much land is within 5 m of a cycling path?

A five-metre buffer is created on both sides of every cycling-path feature. Summing the separate buffer areas double-counts overlaps, so I also dissolve the buffers with st_union() to obtain the unique footprint.

Show the R code 
buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

naive_buffer_ha <- st_area(buffer_cycling) |>
  sum() |>
  set_units("ha")

dissolved_buffer_ha <- buffer_cycling |>
  st_union() |>
  st_area() |>
  set_units("ha")

overlap_pct <- as.numeric(
  (naive_buffer_ha - dissolved_buffer_ha) / naive_buffer_ha * 100
)

buffer_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Sum of individual buffers", "Dissolved unique footprint"),
  `Area (hectares)` = round(c(as.numeric(naive_buffer_ha), as.numeric(dissolved_buffer_ha)), 2),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(buffer_results, caption = "Area within five metres of cycling paths")
Area within five metres of cycling paths
Method Area (hectares)
Sum of individual buffers 498.97
Dissolved unique footprint 431.51

After dissolving the overlaps, the five-metre buffer covers approximately 431.51 hectares. A simple sum gives 498.97 hectares because overlapping buffers are counted more than once. That overstates the unique footprint by about 13.5%.

Question 2: How many pre-schools are in each subzone?

st_intersects() returns the pre-school row indices that fall inside each subzone. lengths() converts that list into one count per subzone.

Show the R code 
mpsz$PreSch_Count <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

top_count <- mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, PreSch_Count) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_Count)) |>
  head(10)

kable(
  top_count,
  col.names = c("Subzone", "Planning area", "Pre-schools"),
  caption = "Subzones with the most pre-schools"
)
Subzones with the most pre-schools
Subzone Planning area Pre-schools
TAMPINES EAST TAMPINES 72
WOODLANDS EAST WOODLANDS 54
ALJUNIED GEYLANG 40
TAMPINES WEST TAMPINES 38
BEDOK NORTH BEDOK 38
FRANKEL BEDOK 36
SENGKANG TOWN CENTRE SENGKANG 33
YUNNAN JURONG WEST 32
HONG KAH JURONG WEST 30
BEDOK SOUTH BEDOK 29

All 2,290 pre-school points were assigned to a subzone. TAMPINES EAST has the highest count, with 72 pre-schools. The median subzone has 4 pre-schools, while some subzones have none.

Pre-school density

Counts favour large residential subzones. Dividing by area shows the number of pre-schools per square kilometre and provides a different view of provision.

Show the R code 
mpsz$Area_sqkm <- st_area(mpsz) |>
  set_units("km^2") |>
  as.numeric()

mpsz$PreSch_Density <- mpsz$PreSch_Count / mpsz$Area_sqkm

top_density <- mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PreSch_Count, Area_sqkm, PreSch_Density) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_Density)) |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(
    Area_sqkm = round(Area_sqkm, 2),
    PreSch_Density = round(PreSch_Density, 2)
  )

kable(
  top_density,
  col.names = c("Subzone", "Pre-schools", "Area (km²)", "Pre-schools per km²"),
  caption = "Subzones with the highest pre-school density"
)
Subzones with the highest pre-school density
Subzone Pre-schools Area (km²) Pre-schools per km²
CECIL 7 0.20 35.60
MANDAI ESTATE 5 0.14 34.93
SEMBAWANG CENTRAL 27 0.96 28.05
PHILLIP 1 0.04 25.36
SERANGOON NORTH 17 0.68 24.83
SENGKANG TOWN CENTRE 33 1.46 22.67
WOODLANDS EAST 54 2.55 21.15
KATONG 22 1.08 20.39
MIDVIEW 19 0.94 20.29
KEAT HONG 23 1.14 20.11

CECIL has the highest density at 35.6 pre-schools per km². This does not mean it has the most facilities: small-area subzones can rank highly even with modest counts. Count is more useful for absolute provision, while density is more useful for provision relative to land area.

Show the R code 
count_map <- ggplot(mpsz) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = PreSch_Count), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Pre-school count by subzone") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")

density_map <- ggplot(mpsz) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = PreSch_Density), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "Per km²") +
  labs(title = "Pre-school density by subzone") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")

count_map
Show the R code 
density_map

Exploratory data analysis

Show the R code 
ggplot(mpsz, aes(x = PreSch_Density)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#4f86c6", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-school density is strongly right-skewed",
    subtitle = "Most subzones have low density; a small number have high values",
    x = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
    y = "Number of subzones"
  )

The histogram has a long right tail. Most subzones have few pre-schools per square kilometre, while a small number have much higher density. This matters for the later thematic map because its appearance will depend on how the skewed values are classified.

What I found

  • The current official spatial files contain 323 subzones, 8,523 cycling-path features, and 2,290 pre-school locations.
  • Transforming from WGS84 to EPSG:3414 is essential before calculating metres or square kilometres.
  • The unique five-metre cycling-path buffer covers about 431.51 hectares.
  • TAMPINES EAST has the most pre-schools (72), while CECIL has the highest density (35.6 per km²).
  • Count and density answer different questions, and density is sensitive to very small subzone areas.

Limitations

The datasets come from different reference dates, so I treat this as a methods exercise rather than a fully time-aligned planning study. A five-metre buffer measures geometric proximity, not construction feasibility or legal land acquisition. Density per land area also does not account for the number or age of children living in each subzone.

## Overview

I worked through [Chapter 1: Geospatial Data Science with R](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap01.html) using the current public downloads. The steps cover importing, checking, projecting, converting and geoprocessing spatial data in R. I use them to answer two practical questions:

1. How much land lies within five metres of Singapore's cycling-path network?
2. How are pre-schools distributed across Master Plan 2014 subzones?

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

pacman::p_load(sf, dplyr, ggplot2, knitr, units)

options(scipen = 999)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

data_path <- "data"
```

## Data and packages

The files now supplied through data.gov.sg are GeoJSON rather than the shapefile and KML formats used in the original course notes. I used GeoJSON because it is the official downloadable format and keeps each layer's geometry in one file.

The requested **Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web)** collection currently has no downloadable child dataset, so I used **Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (No Sea)**. For the pre-school density calculation, this is a reasonable substitute because offshore polygons add area but no pre-school points.

| Dataset | Source | Format | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) | [URA via data.gov.sg](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_226cacceceff94f0c8b814962a5307c9/view) | GeoJSON | Analysis zones |
| Cycling Path Network | [LTA via data.gov.sg](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_8f468b25193f64be8a16fa7d8f60f553/view) | GeoJSON | Buffer analysis |
| Pre-Schools Location | [ECDA via data.gov.sg](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_61eefab99958fd70e6aab17320a71f1c/view) | GeoJSON | Point-in-polygon counts |
| Singapore Airbnb listings, 28 Dec 2024 | [Inside Airbnb](https://beta.insideairbnb.com/get-the-data/) | CSV | Aspatial-to-spatial conversion |

The required packages are loaded with `pacman::p_load()`: `sf` manages spatial data, `dplyr` wrangles tables, `ggplot2` plots the results, `knitr` formats tables, and `units` handles area conversions safely.

## Importing geospatial data

`st_read()` reads all three vector datasets as simple-feature data frames. The course's `chap01/data/...` path belongs to the lecturer's project; the paths below match this repository.

```{r}
#| label: import-spatial-data

mpsz <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "MasterPlan2014SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

cyclingpath <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "CyclingPathNetwork.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

preschool <- st_read(
  file.path(data_path, "geospatial", "PreSchoolsLocation.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)
```

### Inspecting the feature data frames

I first check the number of features, geometry type, attributes and coordinate reference system (CRS).

```{r}
#| label: spatial-data-summary

spatial_summary <- data.frame(
  Object = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  Features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(cyclingpath), nrow(preschool)),
  Attributes = c(ncol(mpsz) - 1, ncol(cyclingpath) - 1, ncol(preschool) - 1),
  Geometry = c(
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(mpsz))), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(cyclingpath))), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(preschool))), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  `Native CRS` = c(st_crs(mpsz)$input, st_crs(cyclingpath)$input, st_crs(preschool)$input),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(spatial_summary, caption = "Imported geospatial datasets")
```

The objects contain polygon, line, and point geometries respectively. All three arrive in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), whose coordinates are measured in degrees.

```{r}
#| label: preview-map
#| fig-cap: "Planning subzones, cycling paths, and pre-school locations before analysis"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mpsz, fill = "#f5f7fa", color = "#b8c2cc", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = cyclingpath, color = "#2a9d8f", linewidth = 0.18, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = preschool, color = "#d1495b", size = 0.25, alpha = 0.55) +
  labs(
    title = "The three spatial layers align in WGS84",
    subtitle = "Subzones (grey), cycling paths (green), and pre-schools (red)"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

## Working with projection

Distance and area should not be calculated in longitude and latitude. I transform all three objects to **SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414)**, a projected CRS measured in metres.

```{r}
#| label: transform-crs

mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, crs = 3414)
cyclingpath <- st_transform(cyclingpath, crs = 3414)
preschool <- st_transform(preschool, crs = 3414)

crs_check <- data.frame(
  Object = c("Planning subzones", "Cycling paths", "Pre-schools"),
  EPSG = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(cyclingpath)$epsg, st_crs(preschool)$epsg),
  Units = c("metres", "metres", "metres")
)

kable(crs_check, caption = "CRS after transformation")
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
`st_transform()` recalculates the coordinates in a new CRS. `st_set_crs()` only changes the CRS label and should be used only when the coordinates were already expressed in that CRS but were labelled incorrectly.
:::

## Importing and converting aspatial data

The Airbnb CSV contains longitude and latitude fields but no geometry column, so it begins as an ordinary data frame.

```{r}
#| label: import-aspatial-data

listings <- read.csv(
  file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "listings.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

listings_sf <- st_as_sf(
  listings,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
) |>
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

listing_summary <- data.frame(
  Records = nrow(listings_sf),
  Geometry = paste(unique(as.character(st_geometry_type(listings_sf))), collapse = ", "),
  EPSG = st_crs(listings_sf)$epsg,
  `Longitude/latitude retained` = all(c("longitude", "latitude") %in% names(listings_sf)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(listing_summary, caption = "Airbnb data after conversion to a spatial object")
```

The coordinate order is `longitude, latitude` (x, y). Reversing it would place the observations far outside Singapore. The converted object contains `r format(nrow(listings_sf), big.mark = ",")` point features in EPSG:3414.

## Geoprocessing

### Question 1: How much land is within 5 m of a cycling path?

A five-metre buffer is created on both sides of every cycling-path feature. Summing the separate buffer areas double-counts overlaps, so I also dissolve the buffers with `st_union()` to obtain the unique footprint.

```{r}
#| label: cycling-buffer

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

naive_buffer_ha <- st_area(buffer_cycling) |>
  sum() |>
  set_units("ha")

dissolved_buffer_ha <- buffer_cycling |>
  st_union() |>
  st_area() |>
  set_units("ha")

overlap_pct <- as.numeric(
  (naive_buffer_ha - dissolved_buffer_ha) / naive_buffer_ha * 100
)

buffer_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Sum of individual buffers", "Dissolved unique footprint"),
  `Area (hectares)` = round(c(as.numeric(naive_buffer_ha), as.numeric(dissolved_buffer_ha)), 2),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(buffer_results, caption = "Area within five metres of cycling paths")
```

After dissolving the overlaps, the five-metre buffer covers approximately **`r round(as.numeric(dissolved_buffer_ha), 2)` hectares**. A simple sum gives `r round(as.numeric(naive_buffer_ha), 2)` hectares because overlapping buffers are counted more than once. That overstates the unique footprint by about `r round(overlap_pct, 1)`%.

### Question 2: How many pre-schools are in each subzone?

`st_intersects()` returns the pre-school row indices that fall inside each subzone. `lengths()` converts that list into one count per subzone.

```{r}
#| label: preschool-counts

mpsz$PreSch_Count <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

top_count <- mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, PreSch_Count) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_Count)) |>
  head(10)

kable(
  top_count,
  col.names = c("Subzone", "Planning area", "Pre-schools"),
  caption = "Subzones with the most pre-schools"
)
```

All `r format(sum(mpsz$PreSch_Count), big.mark = ",")` pre-school points were assigned to a subzone. **`r top_count$SUBZONE_N[1]` has the highest count, with `r top_count$PreSch_Count[1]` pre-schools.** The median subzone has `r median(mpsz$PreSch_Count)` pre-schools, while some subzones have none.

### Pre-school density

Counts favour large residential subzones. Dividing by area shows the number of pre-schools per square kilometre and provides a different view of provision.

```{r}
#| label: preschool-density

mpsz$Area_sqkm <- st_area(mpsz) |>
  set_units("km^2") |>
  as.numeric()

mpsz$PreSch_Density <- mpsz$PreSch_Count / mpsz$Area_sqkm

top_density <- mpsz |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PreSch_Count, Area_sqkm, PreSch_Density) |>
  arrange(desc(PreSch_Density)) |>
  head(10) |>
  mutate(
    Area_sqkm = round(Area_sqkm, 2),
    PreSch_Density = round(PreSch_Density, 2)
  )

kable(
  top_density,
  col.names = c("Subzone", "Pre-schools", "Area (km²)", "Pre-schools per km²"),
  caption = "Subzones with the highest pre-school density"
)
```

**`r top_density$SUBZONE_N[1]` has the highest density at `r top_density$PreSch_Density[1]` pre-schools per km².** This does not mean it has the most facilities: small-area subzones can rank highly even with modest counts. Count is more useful for absolute provision, while density is more useful for provision relative to land area.

```{r}
#| label: preschool-maps
#| fig-cap: "Absolute pre-school count and density tell different stories"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

count_map <- ggplot(mpsz) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = PreSch_Count), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Pre-school count by subzone") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")

density_map <- ggplot(mpsz) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = PreSch_Density), color = "white", linewidth = 0.08) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", name = "Per km²") +
  labs(title = "Pre-school density by subzone") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")

count_map
density_map
```

## Exploratory data analysis

```{r}
#| label: density-histogram
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of pre-school density across subzones"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(mpsz, aes(x = PreSch_Density)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#4f86c6", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-school density is strongly right-skewed",
    subtitle = "Most subzones have low density; a small number have high values",
    x = "Pre-schools per square kilometre",
    y = "Number of subzones"
  )
```

The histogram has a long right tail. Most subzones have few pre-schools per square kilometre, while a small number have much higher density. This matters for the later thematic map because its appearance will depend on how the skewed values are classified.

## What I found

- The current official spatial files contain `r nrow(mpsz)` subzones, `r format(nrow(cyclingpath), big.mark = ",")` cycling-path features, and `r format(nrow(preschool), big.mark = ",")` pre-school locations.
- Transforming from WGS84 to EPSG:3414 is essential before calculating metres or square kilometres.
- The unique five-metre cycling-path buffer covers about **`r round(as.numeric(dissolved_buffer_ha), 2)` hectares**.
- **`r top_count$SUBZONE_N[1]`** has the most pre-schools (`r top_count$PreSch_Count[1]`), while **`r top_density$SUBZONE_N[1]`** has the highest density (`r top_density$PreSch_Density[1]` per km²).
- Count and density answer different questions, and density is sensitive to very small subzone areas.

## Limitations

The datasets come from different reference dates, so I treat this as a methods exercise rather than a fully time-aligned planning study. A five-metre buffer measures geometric proximity, not construction feasibility or legal land acquisition. Density per land area also does not account for the number or age of children living in each subzone.
